claims.text: Controlled heat treatment of low-alloy steel can generate uniformly distributed fine carbide precipitates.
The precipitated carbides locally sequester chromium and molybdenum.
Local sequestration of chromium and molybdenum promotes formation and maintenance of a robust, self-healing passive oxide film.
The robust, self-healing passive oxide film enhances corrosion resistance under chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions.
The as-received baseline steel lacks engineered fine carbide precipitates.
Heat treatment at approximately 700 degrees Celsius for programmed durations encourages fine, uniformly distributed carbide or intermetallic precipitation.
Quenching locks in the precipitate-containing microstructure produced by the heat treatment.
The engineered precipitates pin grain boundaries.
The engineered precipitates maintain local compositional homogeneity.
Grain-boundary pinning and local compositional homogeneity enable formation of a continuous, robust passive oxide film.
The passive oxide film self-heals after minor damage.
The continuous, self-healing passive film inhibits pit initiation and propagation.
Heat-treated steel will have a lower pit-initiation frequency than untreated steel.
Heat-treated steel will exhibit less weight loss during long-term immersion than untreated steel.
Heat-treated steel will have a higher proportion of protective, self-healing passive oxide film than untreated steel.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to low-alloy steels of similar composition and microstructure under standard chemical-processing and simulated nuclear environments.
Changes in alloy chemistry or exposure to extreme environments may alter the effectiveness of the proposed passivation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The precipitates are said to locally sequester chromium and molybdenum while also maintaining local compositional homogeneity. Sequestration implies partitioning between precipitates and the surrounding matrix, so the asserted homogeneity is internally in tension unless the relevant spatial scale or matrix composition is defined.
